title: Dell’s earning report was bullish for Intel CPU demand, analyst says
detail:
Dell’s earning report was bullish for Intel CPU demand, analyst says
Frank DeMatteo
Fri, September 4, 2026 at 10:21 AM CDT 4 min read
INTC
DELL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing.com -- Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) could reach $200 per share as surging AI workloads drive what Global Equities Research analyst Trip Chowdhry estimates is 16-fold year-over-year growth in CPU demand. Chowdhry published a note arguing that Dell's most recent earnings call provides direct validation of that thesis, pointing to Dell's traditional server revenue rising 122% year-over-year as evidence of accelerating Intel CPU adoption.

Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) is the most direct equity expression of the structural shift Chowdhry describes. The firm's $200 price target and a 2031 EPS estimate of $20 rest on three interlocking arguments: rising CPU-to-GPU ratios in AI clusters, x86's entrenched enterprise position, and the architectural advantages of Intel's Clearwater Forest processor.

Dell's Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke supplied language that Chowdhry seized on. Clarke said on the earnings call that Dell is seeing "demand for new servers that have more cores" and separately described "a growing trend of customers that require meaningful CPU compute capacity to support AI and agentic workflows." Clarke also noted that traditional server revenue "was up 122% as demand remains exceptionally strong." Chowdhry's note states plainly: "This is INTC CPUs."

The demand driver, in Global Equities Research's telling, is a medium-level shift in AI training workloads. "INTC CPUs are seeing 16x y-y growth as Training shifts to Heavy Media - Video, Images and Audio from simple Text," Chowdhry wrote. Processing video, images, and audio is far more compute-intensive than training on text alone, and CPUs are bearing a growing share of that burden alongside GPUs.

The CPU-to-GPU ratio inversion underpins much of the bull case. Two generations ago, Chowdhry notes, one CPU could manage eight GPUs. Today, according to Global Equities Research, it takes two to four CPUs just to keep pace with a single GPU or TPU. That structural change alone implies a multi-fold increase in CPU unit demand per AI server rack, independent of any market-share gains Intel makes against AMD.

On the competitive landscape, Intel's Clearwater Forest leads the core-count comparison that Chowdhry lays out. Clearwater Forest offers 576 cores, versus AMD's Turin Dense at 192 cores and Nvidia's Vera Rubin at 88 cores, which began shipping in August 2026 per Global Equities Research's summary. Chowdhry frames Nvidia's Vera Rubin and Grace products as "GPU Controllers" rather than true CPU competitors, suggesting the two markets are less head-to-head than commonly assumed.

title: Intel Witnesses an Uptrend in Estimate Revisions: Is it Worth Buying?
detail:
Intel Witnesses an Uptrend in Estimate Revisions: Is it Worth Buying?
Aritra Chatterjee
Fri, September 4, 2026 at 9:57 AM CDT 4 min read
INTC
ARM
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Earnings estimates for Intel Corporation INTC for 2026 and 2027 have moved up 44.12% to $1.47 and 35.42% to $1.95, respectively, over the past 60 days. The positive estimate revisions depict bullish sentiments about the stock's growth potential.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

INTC Rides on Strong AI Traction, Improving Manufacturing Execution

Data Center and AI (DCAI) is emerging as one of Intel's strongest growth engines for the company. DCAI revenue increased 59% year over year to $6.3 billion in the second quarter, supported by strong demand from hyperscale and enterprise customers. Strong server CPU demand and growing adoption of Xeon 6 processors are expected to fuel growth in upcoming quarters.

Intel is rapidly broadening its traditional PC offerings by incorporating AI capabilities. AI PC revenues are up 26% sequentially and represent about two-thirds of segment revenues. At Hot Chips 2026, Intel detailed Wildcat Lake, launched as Intel Core Series 3, for laptops and intelligent edge platforms. Built on Intel 18A, it combines CPU cores, Xe3 graphics with XMX acceleration and an NPU delivering up to 17 TOPS, while marking Intel's first use of UCIe in a processor. Intel has secured 130 Series 3 edge AI design wins, and edge deployments account for 10% of CCPG revenue.

Intel is expanding beyond general-purpose CPUs into customized silicon designed for specific workloads. In the second quarter of fiscal 2026, purpose-built silicon revenue increased about 20% sequentially and nearly tripled year over year, reaching an estimated $2 billion run rate, with management targeting $4 billion in the not-too-distant future.

Operational improvements are providing another potential earnings driver. Intel is seeing better yields, faster cycle times and higher factory output across several process nodes. In the second quarter, higher revenue, improved yields and pricing contributed to a non-GAAP gross margin of 41.8%, while operating cash flow reached $7 billion.

Supply Constraints, Stiff Competition, Weak PC Market are Concerns

Intel is dealing with a difficult supply environment even as demand remains strong. Industry-wide shortages of leading-edge wafers, memory and substrates are limiting the company's ability to fully capitalize on the growing customer requirements. Management expects PC consumption to decline at a low-double-digit rate in 2026, citing higher memory prices and supply constraints.

Intel operates in an industry characterized by aggressive competition and rapid technological change. It faces competition from Advanced Micro Devices AMD and Arm Holdings ARM in server CPUs. The broader AI infrastructure market remains highly contested across CPUs, GPUs, ASICs and networking. Intel's confidence in catching up and later leapfrogging competitors depends on timely execution across Clearwater Forest, Diamond Rapids and Coral Rapids.

Intel's global manufacturing and supply chain expose it to geopolitical and trade-related risks. The company specifically highlights tensions involving the United States and China, developments around Taiwan, tariffs and export controls as factors that could disrupt operations.

title: How Far AMD Stock Can Swing In Its Calm Case
detail:
How Far AMD Stock Can Swing In Its Calm Case
Trefis Team
Fri, September 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM CDT 3 min read
Image from Pixabay

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) trades at about $456.16, and its option chain has already put numbers on how far the stock can travel from here. Over roughly the next 380 days that chain marks out a band running from $260 to $792.23. The width is what matters if you hold the shares. That is the risk you are carrying, whichever way it breaks.

A Two-In-Three Chance Of Landing Between $260 And $792

From $456.16, the $792.23 ceiling sits about 73.7% higher and the $260 floor about 43.0% lower. Neither end is a forecast. The chain prices roughly a two-in-three chance of finishing inside the band, leaving about a 16% chance above the ceiling and about a 16% chance below the floor.

In your own money, that is more than 40% of the position at risk on the downside, against a gain of close to three quarters at the other end. The two ends are not equally far from here because a stock cannot fall below zero but can rise without limit. That asymmetry is also why the $260 put costs $12.25 while the $790 call costs $33.92, which says nothing about where the market thinks this goes.

AMD Has Already Moved More Than This

AMD's realized volatility over the trailing year was 71.8%. The implied volatility quoted on those year-out options is 54.1%, running at 0.75 times it. Separately, a broad reading of AMD implied volatility sits in the 13th percentile of its own trailing one-year range. Options usually charge more than history justifies. Here they are charging less.

The recent past has not been calm. AMD has returned 181.4% over the trailing twelve months, and it still trades about 21% below its 52-week high after giving back 12.8% over the trailing three months. So the $260-to-$792.23 span is what a market expecting things to settle down still leaves open.

The Ramp That Sits Under Both Ends Of That Band

The width is a ramp problem. Helios, the rack-scale platform that pairs Instinct GPUs with EPYC CPUs, is in production, with initial shipments due to begin in the third quarter of 2026 and a ramp into 2027. The commitments behind it land later: one customer has agreed to deploy up to 2 gigawatts of MI450 series GPUs in Helios, the first gigawatt from the first half of 2027. Management expects data center segment revenue to more than double year-over-year in 2027.

None of that has reached the income statement yet, and the nearer picture cuts both ways. Gaming revenue fell 31% year-over-year on the console cycle. Management is planning for a softer PC market as memory and component costs rise, though it expects its own client business to outperform that market, and calls the server CPU supply chain tight now while expecting 2027 supply to be better than 2026. A ramp of that size either arrives or slips, and either way the range stays wide.

title: QCOM Showered Owners With Cash. The Stock Still Lagged The Market
detail:
QCOM Showered Owners With Cash. The Stock Still Lagged The Market
Trefis Team

^GSPC
INTC
TXN
SPGI

Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

The chipmaker showered its owners with cash while the stock price went nowhere fast, raising a sharp question about what all that money actually bought.

Qualcomm (QCOM) stock has been a study in contrasts. While the chip designer's name is a fixture in tech headlines, its shares trade around $168.57, some 32% below their two-year high. Yet behind the stock chart, a different story has been unfolding: a torrent of cash returned to owners. Over the last five years, Qualcomm handed back $44 billion through dividends and buybacks, a figure equal to 25% of its entire market value. The paradox is stark. The company returned a fortune, but holding the stock produced a total return of just +33% over that period, while the S&P 500 delivered +85%. This raises the central question for any owner: was the cash worth the chronic underperformance, and is it a rational bet from here?

The cash machine is built on more than just phones.

That $44 billion payout is the 35th largest among all U.S. companies, dwarfing the $5.8 billion returned by the median S&P 500 firm. The engine behind it is a business that generated $10.42 billion in free cash flow over the last twelve months. The money flows from two primary sources: the QCT segment that sells its Snapdragon chips for handsets, cars, and connected devices, and the highly profitable QTL licensing division.

Of the total returned, $18 billion arrived as dividends and $26 billion was used for share repurchases. Now, management is pointing to a future where the reliance on handsets shrinks. The company has laid out a target to grow its non-handset revenue to "$40 billion by fiscal 2029," a dramatic pivot toward automotive, IoT, and the data center.

But is this a reward for patience or a sign of a business out of better ideas?

Here is the uncomfortable math for shareholders. The cash returned is cash not reinvested in the business to drive faster growth. This is the classic trade-off. For Qualcomm, it comes at a critical moment. The company is attempting a large and expensive diversification into new markets just as it faces new pressures. A recent Trefis analysis, for instance, asks what happens to Qualcomm stock if the new revenue earns less.

The honest catch is that this pivot carries immense execution risk. Management acknowledges its "data center business is just at the beginning of its journey," and that these new custom chip deals are expected to be "significantly lower" margin than its baseline business. This expansion is happening while a key piece of its legacy business is shrinking faster than expected, with management noting its share in the upcoming iPhone launch is "expected to be materially lower than our prior estimate of 20%." For investors who prefer the broader semiconductor theme to a single company's turnaround story, a semiconductor ETF like SMH offers a different way to participate.

Despite this rise in the stock price, Super Micro Computer offers to its investors at current levels. The undervaluation is further substantiated by Zacks Value Score of B.

SMCI Forward-12 Month (P/S) Valuation Chart
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

SMCI Gains From Partnership With Leading Chip Companies

Super Micro Computer is increasingly positioning itself as a complete AI infrastructure provider rather than a conventional server manufacturer. SMCI's close collaboration with leading AI-chip vendors, including Intel INTC, NVIDIA NVDA and Advanced Micro Devices AMD, enables the company to align system designs with their product-release schedules, helping SMCI accelerate time-to-market and reduce system-level issues.

SMCI is shipping volume systems based on the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, HGX B300, B200 NVL4 and RTX 6000 Pro platforms, while preparing first-to-market systems for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin VRNVL72, Rubin HGX and Vera C1 platforms. With Advanced Micro Devices, SMCI launched the complete Helios product line and MI450 Total Solution, alongside continued momentum for EPYC CPUs and MI350 and MI355X platforms.

The breadth of these partnerships strengthens SMCI's position as AI infrastructure evolves from individual GPU servers toward complete rack-scale deployments. The company's NVIDIA and Advanced Micro Devices platforms can be integrated into its Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS), which combine compute, storage, networking, power, direct liquid cooling, software and services.

SMCI is also scaling the infrastructure required to support these partner platforms. Its fiscal 2027 plan calls for more than 6,000 racks of monthly capacity, split between roughly 3,000 direct-liquid-cooled and 3,000 air-cooled racks, with 240kW racks expected to enter volume production and 500kW systems approaching. The company's DCBBS portfolio also includes cooling distribution units, chilled doors, power shelves, battery backup, switches and data-center management software giving customers one shop stop advantage.

SMCI Benefits From Record Backlog and Rising Shipments

SMCI's fiscal 2026 revenues nearly doubled to $39.1 billion, while the company generated more than $60 billion in new orders during the fourth quarter, taking the backlog to record levels entering fiscal 2027. The AI solutions represented about 60% of SMCI's fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues because several large projects shifted timing, but management expects AI-related solutions to exceed 80% of revenue going forward based on backlog.
